title: Dynamic hydration-driven self-activation of a perovskite cathode for protonic ceramic fuel cells
content: The development of high-performance cathodes remains a critical challenge for protonic ceramic fuel cells (PCFCs). Here, we report that harnessing the dynamic evolution of the surface and defect chemistry of perovskite cathodes enables electrochemical self-activation without detectable structural reconstruction under operation, markedly enhancing cell performance. As a representative example, Pr1.2Ba0.8Co0.8Fe0.8Mn0.4O5+δ delivers an 87% increase in peak power density after continuous cyclic voltammetry, reaching 1.44 W cm−2 at 650 °C with long-term stability over 600 h. Combined electrochemical and spectroscopic analyses reveal that this self-activation originates from hydration-driven proton uptake. Cathodic polarization, coupled with oxygen consumption (or low oxygen pressure) and in situ-generated H2O, induces Mn/Co reduction, increases oxygen-defect concentration, and promotes surface hydroxylation. This process effectively expands the electrochemically active region beyond the electrolyte–cathode interface. In situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy directly captures spontaneous hydroxylation under low oxygen pressure and humid conditions, confirming the hydration process, while theoretical calculations show that Mn-induced local coordination lowers the hydration energy and favors proton uptake at elevated temperatures. This work not only presents a high-performance PCFC cathode but also establishes a new design strategy that exploits dynamic surface and defect evolution to achieve enhanced electrochemical performance.
